procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Delhi at New Delhi
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 24.11.2022 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi in BA No.313 of 2022, specifically clause (e) of paragraph 9.0.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant approached the High Court seeking an order under section 438 of the Cr. PC (anticipatory bail). The High Court granted bail to the appellant and the builder by a common order dated 24th November, 2022, but imposed a condition that the appellant had volunteered to keep in deposit Rs. 22,00,000/- (Rupees twenty-two lakh). The appellant also applied for and was granted an extension of time by the High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant is aggrieved by the condition imposed by the High Court (clause (e) of paragraph 9.0) and seeks its revocation while wanting the rest of the High Court's order to be maintained. The State opposed the appeal, arguing that the condition was based on the appellant's voluntary undertaking and subsequent application for extension of time. The complainants also filed an application for intervention, seeking to assist the Court, which was dismissed.

directions: The appeal stands disposed of on terms as aforesaid.
The application for intervention stands dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the condition of depositing a substantial amount of money for the grant of anticipatory bail is sustainable in law and within the purview of Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure?

facts: The issue arose from cases where High Courts, while granting anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.), imposed a condition requiring the accused to deposit a substantial sum of money.
In one instance, an appellant accused of cheating was ordered to deposit Rs. 1,00,00,000 in a fixed deposit in the complainant's name as a prerequisite for bail.
In another case, the High Court directed the deposit of Rs. 41 lakhs, which the Supreme Court viewed as virtually issuing a recovery order typical of a civil suit.
These cases typically involved private disputes, such as cheating allegations between private parties over financial transactions.
law: Section 438(2) of the Cr.P.C. empowers courts to impose conditions when granting anticipatory bail.
The primary purpose of bail conditions is to ensure the accused's appearance for investigation and trial, facilitate an unhindered investigation, and protect community safety.
Conditions imposed must not be harsh, onerous, unreasonable, or excessive, as this would frustrate the very object of anticipatory bail, which is to protect personal liberty.
The accused is presumed innocent until proven guilty, and the right to personal freedom should not be dependent on compliance with unreasonable restrictions.
Criminal proceedings for bail should not be transformed into a process for the recovery of money, which is the domain of civil courts.
application: The Supreme Court reasoned that making the deposit of a large sum of money a pre-condition for bail is fundamentally onerous and unreasonable.
It found that such a condition creates the improper impression that bail can be secured simply by depositing the money alleged to have been cheated, which is not the purpose of bail provisions.
The Court held that by imposing such conditions, the criminal court was effectively acting as a civil court for recovery, which is an incorrect use of its jurisdiction under Section 438.

The Court distinguished between private disputes and cases involving public money. It stated that while a voluntary offer to deposit misappropriated public funds might be considered in exceptional cases for the larger public interest, this approach is not warranted in private cheating cases.

Ultimately, the Court determined that requiring a deposit of Rs. 1 crore before the accused's guilt was even established at trial was an excessive condition that frustrated the purpose of anticipatory bail.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the condition of depositing a substantial amount of money for the grant of anticipatory bail is generally not sustainable in law. It held that such conditions are onerous, unreasonable, and fall outside the intended purview of Section 438 of the Cr.P.C., as they improperly convert a criminal proceeding into a civil recovery mechanism and frustrate the object of protecting personal liberty.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the condition of depositing a substantial amount of money for the grant of anticipatory bail is sustainable in law and within the purview of Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure?
appellant_arguments: The appellant's counsel relied on the precedent set in Munish Bhasin (supra) to argue against the condition of depositing a substantial amount for bail.
respondent_arguments: The condition was imposed because the appellant, through his counsel, had voluntarily offered to deposit Rs. 22,00,000 without prejudice to his rights.
The High Court based its order on this undertaking.
The appellant had subsequently applied for and was granted an extension of time to comply with the condition, which makes it inappropriate for the Supreme Court to interfere.

cases.case_name: Gurbaksh Singh Sibbia and others vs. State of Punjab
cases.principle: To meet the challenge of Article 21 of the Constitution, the procedure established by law for depriving a person of his liberty must be fair, just and reasonable. Section 438 (anticipatory bail) is not unjust or unfair, and courts should avoid reading words into it which are not to be found therein.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The provided text does not contain the reasoning or the legal rule of the case. It only includes citations and procedural information.
obiter: No obiter dicta were found in the provided text.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court fell in grave error by imposing a condition precedent for the grant of bail that required the appellant to deposit a substantial sum of money, even if the appellant had made an undertaking to do so. This is because the dispute is predominantly civil in nature, and the criminal law process cannot be used as a mechanism for settling civil disputes or enforcing monetary recovery between private parties.
legal_tests_applied: The words ‘any condition’ used in the provision [Section 438] should not be regarded as conferring absolute power on a court of law to impose any condition that it chooses to impose. Any condition has to be interpreted as a reasonable condition acceptable in the facts permissible in the circumstance and effective in the pragmatic sense and should not defeat the order of grant of bail.
To stand the challenge of Article 21 of the Constitution, the procedure established by law for depriving a person of his liberty must be fair, just and reasonable.
why_respondent_won: The process of criminal law cannot be pressed into service for settling a civil dispute, as the nature of the dispute between the parties is predominantly civil.

Even if the appellant were convicted of the alleged offence, he may not be under any obligation to repay the amount allegedly received from the complainants, making a pre-emptive deposit for bail improper.

The High Court fell in grave error in proceeding on the basis of the undertaking of the appellant and imposing payment of Rs.22,00,000/- (Rupees twenty-two lakh) as a condition precedent for grant of bail.
The facts and circumstances of the case do not warrant such an extreme condition to be imposed.
policy_considerations: While willingness to deposit money may be considered in exceptional cases involving the misappropriation of public money to serve a larger public interest, such an approach is not warranted in cases of private disputes where private parties complain of their money being involved in the offence of cheating.
While deciding a bail application, it is not the jurisdiction of the court to decide civil disputes as between the parties.
